analysis.one_liner: Opens a protected Alaska wildlife refuge to oil and gas drilling, sharing the revenue with Alaska and rural energy programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it died in subcommittees when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have overridden the 1980 law that bars oil and gas drilling on the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, ordering the Interior Department to start leasing there right away [S2][S3]. Money from the leases — royalties and federal income taxes on the oil and gas sold — would have gone into a new trust fund: half to the state of Alaska, a quarter to rural business loan guarantees, and a quarter to biomass research [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced in July 2008, when gas prices were a top national concern, and was backed by 30 House members [S1][S4]. It never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, who would gain the legal right to bid on leases in a refuge that federal law has closed to drilling since 1980 [S2][S3]. The state of Alaska would receive half of all royalties and drilling-related federal income taxes, and rural lenders and biomass researchers would receive the other half through Agriculture Department programs [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies, Alaska, rural bioenergy programs

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Interior Secretary to promptly begin an oil and gas leasing program on the Coastal Plain of Alaska and declares drilling there a compatible use of the wildlife refuge, overriding the statutory prohibition [S2][S3].

Creates an Energy Independence Trust Fund funded by lease royalties and federal income taxes on oil and gas sold from those leases, with 50% paid to Alaska, 25% to rural business and industry loan guarantees, and 25% to the Biomass Research and Development Initiative [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the public would have borne the environmental risk of industrial development inside a national wildlife refuge, and future generations would have lost the option of keeping one of the country's largest undeveloped wild areas intact. The revenue stream promised to rural programs was entirely contingent on how much oil was actually found and produced [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via the refuge's environment

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals section 1003 of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, the provision that expressly prohibits leasing in the refuge, and deems drilling a compatible use — removing the legal barriers that have protected the coastal plain since 1980 [S3].

New leases in the Arctic typically take years to explore and develop, so the bill's promise of relief from high gas prices in 2008 would not have produced oil for consumers in any near term, and the rural energy funding it promises depends entirely on future production actually occurring [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real revenue split to Alaska and rural energy programs, but those benefits flow only if drilling happens in one of the nation's most sensitive protected wild areas, and the bill's main effect — its reason for existing — is to open that area to oil companies. The environmental cost is permanent and the energy-price benefit is speculative and distant; the funding for rural programs could be provided directly without the trade.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees, split among three subcommittees, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Rogers of Alabama introduced the FREE Act on July 31, 2008, with 29 original cosponsors, nearly all Republicans, during a period of high gasoline prices [S1][S3][S4].

It was referred to the Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees and then to subcommittees on Energy and Mineral Resources and on Conservation, Credit, Energy, and Research, among others, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died without ever reaching the House floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the status quo held: the Arctic refuge coastal plain remained closed to leasing, and the oil industry gained nothing from this effort. Alaska and rural energy programs also received nothing, since their promised share depended entirely on drilling that never began.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The refuge stayed closed; oil companies gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Mike D. Rogers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 29 original cosponsors

against.name: Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in subcommittees until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican — 27 of 30 cosponsors were Republicans, with 3 Democrats — in a House controlled by Democrats, and the Democratic-led committees took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain — closed to leasing by statute since 1980 — to oil and gas leasing, a major new access opportunity for the industry [S2][S3]. The public would receive half the royalties and drilling-related taxes through Alaska and rural programs, but would bear the environmental risk of development inside a refuge, and any effect on consumer fuel prices would be years away [S2][S3].
Alaska would receive 50% of all lease royalties and drilling-related federal income taxes deposited into the new trust fund [S2][S3].

Half the fund would finance USDA rural business and industry loan guarantees and a quarter would fund the Biomass Research and Development Initiative — benefits that depend entirely on drilling revenue materializing [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Wildlife refuge conservation and recreation interests
industries.note: Development of the coastal plain, declared a compatible use under the bill, would end the protected status that has shielded the area since 1980, a loss borne by the public's shared natural heritage [S3].
